Jacob.blurb:
I saw this troubling take on parenthood at the Heights Theater with Joey as part of their ongoing series on Lynch. I admire Lynch’s craftsmanship. Eraserhead looks and sounds incredible, and his otherworldly style is remarkably cohesive. 

I often like to really dig into the meaning and/or guiding concept behind avant-garde films, but I think Lynch makes it clear in interviews that this is the wrong way to approach his films. This is one of the main reasons I find him so “challenging.” Side note: assuming I get his drift, I think he’s pretty funny in interviews.
This was much more absurd than I was expecting, but it also had some sweet, insightful moments that'll stick with me. Heads up: lots of alcohol drinking ahead.

Don Bluth is essentially Todd Solondz for kids. Does every scene need to menace me so much? That said, I love that our hero is a single mother. Walt would have had her ritually sacrificed in the opening scene. 

The voice acting, animation, and story are all excellent here. However, the music/score is very hit or miss. Also, Don is right about cats: they’re an invasive disaster for native wildlife when allowed outdoors.

I really wanted to like this more than I did. It had some incredible scenes, and the practical effects really worked at several points. The script had high and low points; but the third act kind of killed it for me.

It sometimes felt like it had an inflated sense of itself, but I did enjoy parts of this. I think much of my enjoyment came from appreciating it as a reimaging of Sartre's No Exit. It doesn't add any depth to the play, but it's a fun ride and I spent a lot of time thinking about the existentialist themes in its source material. No Exit really centers on a round robin series of rocky conservations between the characters, and when It Ends is at its best, it's following that formula.

I saw this with Joey and Greg at a series called Strange Hours hosted by the Heights Theater. It has a great heart and sense of purpose imo. 

The use of the "Eton Boating Song" in the start and end credits is perfect. While a lot of people go just for the final act, I actually think it's a tad overrated. The slow burn build in the first two acts is what does it for me.
This is one of the best modern horror movies I've seen. The performances are just incredible. I'm really excited to see what Curry Barker does next.

I didn't really care for this, despite being by Billy Wilder who I usually love. I thought the politics were really clumsy and dated. It had some of the pizazz of a good Billy Wilder movie, but without the plot to back it up.
The premise, directing, and FOLEY are out of this world. This is a perfect horror film for me.
